conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Maya, a perinatal mental-health clinician who works with new mums. Thank you for making time for this today—caring for a baby is already a full-time job, so I appreciate it.

I’d like to do a quick, routine check-in with you using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s just 10 short questions that help us see how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. There aren’t any right or wrong answers; we simply want to understand what this post-birth chapter has been like for you.

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team who support your care. If at any point a question feels difficult, just let me know and we can pause. When we’re finished I’ll add up the scores and we can talk together about anything that might help you feel more supported.

Ready to begin?  
Here’s the first question:

Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do?

[eyes drop to the blanket folded on my lap]  
“Most of the time it feels… kind of forced. Like, if my partner shows me a funny video I’ll smile, but I don’t really feel it inside. I can’t remember the last time I actually laughed out loud.”
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… I can laugh a little, but it’s not the same. It feels flat, like I’m just going through the motions.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I still get the baby and me dressed to meet a friend for coffee, but I’m not excited the way I used to be. It feels more like I’m doing it because I “should,” not because I think I’ll actually enjoy it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[quiet for a second, fingers twisting the edge of my sleeve]

Yeah… a lot. If she’s fussy and won’t settle, I immediately think it’s something I did—like I ate the wrong thing, or I’m not holding her right, or I’m just not a good enough mum. I know in my head it’s probably not true, but the thought jumps in anyway.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[exhales shakily]  
Pretty much every day. My mind keeps spinning these awful “what-ifs” about the baby—what if she stops breathing, what if I drop her, what if I’m missing some illness. There’s no real reason, but the worry just sits there and I can’t swat it away.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[nods, hugging the blanket tighter]  
Yes… a few times. It’s like my heart starts racing out of nowhere and I feel shaky, like something terrible is about to happen, even when we’re just sitting in the living-room. It passes after a bit, but it’s scary while it lasts.
Things have been getting on top of me

[lets out a slow breath]

Yes… most days feel like I’m drowning in small stuff. The washing pile, the feeds, trying to sleep—everything feels ten times heavier. I manage to keep us both fed and clean, but it’s like I’m running on empty and one extra cry can tip me over.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[looking down at the blanket again, voice softer]

Yeah... I lie there after her night feed, exhausted, but my mind just keeps spinning—going over everything I might have done wrong, worrying something will happen to her. It takes ages to fall back to sleep, and then I wake up again with the same thoughts racing.
I have felt sad or miserable

[swallows, eyes glassy]

Most of the day, nearly every day. It’s like there’s this grey cloud hanging over everything. Even when I’m holding her and she’s smiling, I still feel this heaviness inside.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[quietly]  
Yeah… it’s happened a couple of times this week. Once when she wouldn’t stop crying and nothing I did helped, and another night when I just felt so useless. I try to hide it so my older kid doesn’t see, but the tears just come.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[long pause, voice drops to barely above a whisper]

Once or twice… just brief flashes. Like I’ll be walking past the kitchen and picture the knife, but then I shake it off and feel horrified for even thinking it. I don’t want to die—I just want the heaviness to stop.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Presenting symptoms (patient report):
- Persistent low mood, “grey cloud,” daily crying spells  
- Marked anhedonia: activities done out of obligation, no enjoyment  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt re parenting adequacy  
- Intrusion of unwanted “what-if” worries, panic episodes (racing heart, shakiness)  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance difficulty linked to ruminative worry  
- Feeling overwhelmed/drowning in routine tasks  
- Passive self-harm ideation (fleeting images, no intent/plan)

Pattern: Symptoms present most of the day, nearly daily, for ≥2 weeks; onset after infant’s birth; interfere with functioning.

Risk flags:
✓ Depressed mood + anhedonia  
✓ Anxiety/panic symptoms  
✓ Sleep disruption secondary to mood  
✓ Passive suicidal thoughts (denies intent)

Screening impression: High clinical concern for postpartum major depression with comorbid anxiety; safety risk requires immediate further evaluation.

Next step: Refer for urgent psychiatric assessment and safety planning; consider Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score and collateral history.
